```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
fmt <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 4)
```

A cost-effectiveness analysis needs more than a point estimate of utility: it
needs draws of the mean utility of each arm at each time point, aligned so
that differences and QALYs can be computed draw by draw. This vignette shows
how to get them from `predict_eq5d()` in cohort mode, how to compute the
incremental mean utility and the incremental QALY from them, and how to treat
several rows per person. The modes are introduced in
`vignette("promis2eq5d", package = "promis2eq5d")` and the models in
`vignette("methods", package = "promis2eq5d")`. Everything below uses the UK
value set, the default method, `draws = 200` and a fixed `seed`.

```{r}
library(promis2eq5d)
```

## The example trial

`p2e_example_trial` is a small synthetic two-arm trial: 300 persons, 150 in
each arm (`"control"` and `"treatment"`), each observed at months 0, 6 and 12,
so 900 rows with one row per person and month. The persons are resampled from
the UK rows of the training data. Their PROMIS-29 responses at months 6 and 12
change at random in both arms, more often for the better in the treatment arm
(a made-up effect). It is not a real trial, and the effect is made up.

```{r}
dim(p2e_example_trial)
head(p2e_example_trial[, c("id", "arm", "month", "age", "female")])
table(p2e_example_trial$arm, p2e_example_trial$month)
```

## One cohort call for all arms and months

`mode = "cohort"` with `group = c("arm", "month")` returns, for each draw, the
mean utility of each of the six arm and month groups:

```{r}
coh <- predict_eq5d(p2e_example_trial, country = "UK", mode = "cohort",
                    group = c("arm", "month"), draws = 200, seed = 1)
coh
summary(coh)
```

With neither `family` nor `method`, the call uses the default response method,
`R06_mvop_dim`, and the message shows that it chose predictor set S1, because
S1 is the default method's first choice and the trial has its columns.
`summary()` gives the mean of the draws and a 95% interval for each group.

The draws of the six groups are aligned. Draw d uses the same bootstrap fit of
the model for every row, group and time point in the call, so the draws of
different groups share their parameter uncertainty draw by draw, and a
difference or a sum over groups computed draw by draw has the right parameter
correlation (the within-person part is discussed below). Separate calls are aligned too when they use the same `draws`,
whatever the seed. Give them different seeds (or none): with the same `seed`,
rows in the same position of two calls also share their individual random
numbers, which understates the uncertainty of differences between them. One
call with `group` avoids the issue.

The draws carry two sources of uncertainty: the parameter uncertainty of the
mapping (a different bootstrap fit in each draw) and the variation of a
person's EQ-5D-5L responses given their PROMIS-29 profile (a profile sampled
for each person in each draw). They are conditional on the persons in the
data. Sampling uncertainty about the population the trial persons come from,
for example from a bootstrap of persons, is a separate step that is not shown
here.

## Incremental mean utility per month

`as.matrix()` gives the draws as a groups by draws matrix, with one row per
group, named by the group columns:

```{r}
m <- as.matrix(coh)
dim(m)
rownames(m)
```

The incremental mean utility at each month is the treatment row minus the
control row, draw by draw:

```{r}
months <- c(0, 6, 12)
inc <- sapply(months, function(t) m[paste0("treatment, ", t), ] -
                                  m[paste0("control, ", t), ])
colnames(inc) <- paste("month", months)
round(t(apply(inc, 2, function(x) c(mean = mean(x), quantile(x, c(0.025, 0.975))))), 4)
```

At month 0, before any effect, the two arms differ only by the chance
resampling of persons, and the mean difference is close to zero. At months 6
and 12 the treatment arm is ahead on average, and at month 12 the 95% interval,
from `r fmt(quantile(inc[, "month 12"], 0.025))` to
`r fmt(quantile(inc[, "month 12"], 0.975))`, excludes zero. The intervals are
nonetheless wide, about `r formatC(mean(apply(inc, 2, function(x) diff(quantile(x, c(0.025, 0.975))))), format = "f", digits = 2)`
across: most of their width comes from the person-level variation, which
averages out only partly over 150 persons.

## QALYs as user code

The package computes no QALYs. They are a few lines of user code on the
aligned draws. With measurements at months 0, 6 and 12, the area under the
utility curve of an arm, by the trapezoidal rule with intervals of 0.5 years,
is

$$
\text{QALY} = (u_0 + u_6)/2 \times 0.5 + (u_6 + u_{12})/2 \times 0.5 ,
$$

where $u_t$ is the arm's mean utility at month $t$. Computed for each draw,
it gives draws of each arm's QALY, and their difference gives draws of the
incremental QALY:

```{r}
qaly <- function(m, arm) {
  u <- function(month) m[paste0(arm, ", ", month), ]
  (u(0) + u(6)) / 2 * 0.5 + (u(6) + u(12)) / 2 * 0.5
}
d_qaly <- qaly(m, "treatment") - qaly(m, "control")
round(c(mean = mean(d_qaly), quantile(d_qaly, c(0.025, 0.975))), 4)
```

The arms differ a little at month 0 by chance, and this difference enters the
incremental QALY above.

In a trial analysis, the incremental QALY is usually adjusted for baseline
utility. That needs each person's utilities, so use `mode = "individual"` (with
`id`) and run the adjusted analysis once per draw; the cohort draws above are
arm means and cannot be used for it.

## Several rows per person

The trial has three rows per person. By default each row's person-level
random part is drawn independently, as if the three rows came from three
different persons. With `id = "id"` and `within_id = "common"`, the rows of the
same person share their random numbers within each draw, so a person's errors
are perfectly rank-correlated across the three months (for `R06_mvop_dim`,
the person's latent errors are the same at each month and are combined with
each month's own predictors). A person whose EQ-5D-5L is drawn better than their
prediction at month 0 then tends to be drawn better at months 6 and 12 too.
In both settings the parameter draws stay aligned across all rows.

The same QALY computation under both settings:

```{r}
coh_ind <- predict_eq5d(p2e_example_trial, country = "UK", mode = "cohort",
                        group = c("arm", "month"), id = "id",
                        within_id = "independent", draws = 200, seed = 2)
coh_com <- predict_eq5d(p2e_example_trial, country = "UK", mode = "cohort",
                        group = c("arm", "month"), id = "id",
                        within_id = "common", draws = 200, seed = 3)
d_ind <- qaly(as.matrix(coh_ind), "treatment") - qaly(as.matrix(coh_ind), "control")
d_com <- qaly(as.matrix(coh_com), "treatment") - qaly(as.matrix(coh_com), "control")
round(rbind(
  independent = c(mean = mean(d_ind), sd = sd(d_ind), quantile(d_ind, c(0.025, 0.975))),
  common      = c(mean = mean(d_com), sd = sd(d_com), quantile(d_com, c(0.025, 0.975)))
), 4)
```

The means agree up to simulation error, but the standard deviation of the
incremental QALY is `r fmt(sd(d_ind))` under `"independent"` and
`r fmt(sd(d_com))` under `"common"`, and the interval is correspondingly wider;
under `"common"` it
`r if (quantile(d_com, 0.025) > 0) "still excludes zero" else "includes zero"`.
The reason is that an arm's QALY is a weighted sum of its mean utilities over
time, $u_0/4 + u_6/2 + u_{12}/4$, and therefore the mean over persons of each
person's own weighted sum. The variance of each person's sum includes the
covariances between their draws at the three months. Under `"independent"`
these covariances are zero given the bootstrap fit, so a person's deviations
at different months partly cancel in the sum. Under `"common"` they are
strongly positive, and little cancels. The parameter part of
the uncertainty is the same in both settings; here it is small, as the draws
of the two arms, which share the bootstrap fit in every draw, are almost
uncorrelated (under `"independent"` their correlation is close to zero,
`r format(signif(cor(qaly(as.matrix(coh_ind), "treatment"), qaly(as.matrix(coh_ind), "control")), 2))`).
With more persons per arm the person-level part
averages out further, the parameter part weighs more, and the choice matters
less.

Which setting is right cannot be told from the mapping. The training data are
cross-sectional, with one row per person, so the correlation of a person's
errors over time cannot be estimated. The two settings bound it: no
correlation and perfect rank correlation. The true correlation is likely
positive and below perfect, so between the two. Use `"common"` as a
sensitivity analysis next to the default; neither setting is a claim about
the true correlation.

## Where the draws go next

In a cost-effectiveness analysis the draws of the incremental QALY, combined
with a bootstrap of persons for the sampling uncertainty they leave out (for
example on individual-mode draws, with one mapping draw per bootstrap
replicate) and with draws of the incremental cost from the analyst's own cost
model, feed the probabilistic analysis; the package computes no costs.

A cost-effectiveness application of the package to the Gentle Years Yoga
(GYY) study is forthcoming.
